Light bleeding after delivery can be normal lochia, but passing tissue or large clots after 2 weeks with lower abdominal pain may suggest retained placental tissue, womb infection (postpartum endometritis), or secondary postpartum bleeding.  
Danger signs include heavy bleeding or soaking pads, bad-smelling discharge, fever or chills, worsening lower abdominal pain, dizziness/fainting, severe headache/blurred vision, neck stiffness, swollen painful leg, chest pain, or difficulty breathing.  
Lower abdominal pain with fever, foul discharge, or increasing bleeding is not normal and needs urgent hospital review, examination, ultrasound if available, and treatment such as antibiotics or removal of retained tissue if confirmed.  
To reduce risk, women should deliver with skilled attendants, ensure the placenta is checked complete, keep perineal hygiene with clean pads, avoid inserting herbs or unprescribed medicines into the vagina, treat infections early, breastfeed, eat well, and attend postnatal checks.  
Any new mother with these symptoms should go back to the hospital immediately rather than waiting at home.

He should be assessed by a mental health professional such as a child psychologist, psychiatrist, psychiatric nurse, or trained counsellor, especially if symptoms last more than 2 weeks or he talks about death or harming himself.

Medicine is not the first treatment for normal grief, but if a clinician diagnoses severe depression, anxiety, or sleep problems, they may prescribe treatment alongside counselling.
